title: Groupe de Galois motivique : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
This page is the first page of a letter from Grothendieck to Mumford, dated Algiers, 1 November 1965. It continues on the next page, which ends with a P.S. about Mumford's theta functions.

(1) Context. Grothendieck had earlier told Mumford some conjectures about Hodge structures. The most plausible reading is that he had conjectured that polarized Hodge structures, and analytic families of them, are 'algebraic', meaning they come from the cohomology of algebraic varieties (motives). He now retracts them in that form.

(2) Claim derived from Tate's conjecture. Let X be a smooth, connected, simply connected complex scheme. Let V be a polarized holomorphic family of Hodge structures over X^an. If V is algebraic, then V is constant. Reconstructed argument:
- Spread the family out over a finitely generated field.
- The ℓ-adic local system is trivial because π1 is trivial (this needs the profinite completion of the topological π1 to be trivial, which holds here).
- So the Galois representations on the fibres H^*(Y_x) can be identified with one another.
- The Tate conjecture turns the resulting Galois-equivariant identifications into algebraic correspondences, so the fibre motives are all isomorphic.
- Hence the fibre Hodge structures are all isomorphic. Isomorphism classes vary in a countable set, so a continuous family of them is constant.

(3) Counterexamples to the earlier conjecture. Take X to be a homogeneous space under an affine (linear) algebraic group, for example a flag variety or the compact dual of a period domain. Such X carry many non-constant holomorphic polarized families of Hodge structures. So 'every family is algebraic' cannot hold if Tate holds.

Modern reading: these families violate Griffiths transversality, isolated by Griffiths in 1968. Polarized variations that do satisfy transversality over a simply connected quasi-projective base are constant unconditionally, by the theorem of the fixed part / rigidity (Griffiths, Deligne in Hodge II, Schmid). So Grothendieck's Tate-conditional statement is, for genuinely geometric families, a theorem today. His 'easy examples' are precisely the non-horizontal families.

(4) Next page. Grothendieck proposes testing whether even a single Hodge structure can be algebraic when it has even partial degrees, so that the Hodge group G has G_R compact. He conjectures no, unless G is commutative (CM). As a concrete test he asks for a smooth projective surface with H^{1,1} spanned by algebraic cycles (ρ = h^{1,1}) and h^{0,2} ≥ 2.

Why these are the right test cases: for such Hodge structures, for example the transcendental lattice of type (2,0)+(0,2), the period domain is compact and the horizontal tangent bundle vanishes. So they are infinitesimally rigid, the 'zero-dimensional' analogue of the non-geometric families on page 13.
errors: No outright error. 'Algebraic' is left undefined; the argument from Tate also implicitly needs the Hodge conjecture or a motivic formalism to pass from isomorphic Galois representations to isomorphic Hodge structures. 'Tate's conjecture' here should be read as the standard conjectures on algebraic cycles. The examples given are non-horizontal families, which explains, in modern terms, why they cannot be geometric; Grothendieck does not yet identify transversality as the obstruction.

ideas.what: Over a simply connected smooth complex base, an algebraic (motivic) polarized family of Hodge structures must be constant; derived conditionally from the Tate conjecture
ideas.modern_name: Theorem of the fixed part / rigidity of polarized VHS with trivial monodromy
ideas.where_published: This letter is likely printed in Mumford's Selected Papers vol. II (Springer 2010, correspondence with Grothendieck); unsure.

ideas.what: Non-constant holomorphic families of polarized Hodge structures on homogeneous spaces of affine groups exist, so not every family of Hodge structures is algebraic
ideas.modern_name: Non-horizontal families on compact duals / flag domains; Griffiths transversality as the necessary condition for geometric origin
ideas.where_published: Possibly only in the Grothendieck–Mumford correspondence

ideas.what: Question (next page): can a polarized Hodge structure with compact real Hodge group be geometric unless the group is commutative (CM)? Test case: surfaces with ρ = h^{1,1} and p_g ≥ 2
ideas.modern_name: Surfaces with maximal Picard number; Hodge structures of type (n,0,…,0,n) and whether geometric ones must be CM
ideas.usually_credited_to: Beauville ('Some surfaces with maximal Picard number', 2014); Totaro on Hodge structures of type (n,0,…,0,n)

ideas.what: Use of the term 'Hodge group' (G with G_R compact)

missed.claim: In 1965 Grothendieck links three things: the Tate conjecture, rigidity/constancy of algebraic families over simply connected bases, and the existence of non-geometric analytic families of Hodge structures on homogeneous spaces. This anticipates, conditionally, the fixed-part theorem, and implicitly the role of Griffiths transversality, before Griffiths' 1968 papers.
missed.quote: if X is a smooth, connected simply connected scheme over C, and V a polarized complex analytic family of Hodge structures parametrized by X^hol, then V is "algebraic" only if it is a constant family
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historically shows that the question 'which Hodge structures and families are motivic' was posed by Grothendieck to Mumford in 1965. This bears on the prehistory of Mumford–Tate groups and the motivic Galois group. Probably known to readers of the published correspondence.

missed.claim: On the next page Grothendieck conjectures that a geometric Hodge structure with compact real Hodge group must have commutative Hodge group (CM). He asks for surfaces with ρ = h^{1,1} and p_g ≥ 2, a question studied much later (Beauville 2014), apparently without reference to Grothendieck.
missed.quote: do you know an algebraic smooth projective surface Y over C, such that H^{11}(Y,C) is spanned by algebraic cycles, and dim H^{0,2}(Y,C) ≥ 2 ??
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Gives Grothendieck priority for the maximal-Picard-number / compact-Hodge-group-implies-CM question. Whether geometric Hodge structures with compact Hodge group are always CM remains of interest.

deep.surprise_reason: A clear and early (1965) formulation of the conditional rigidity statement and of non-geometric Hodge families, plus a question later studied independently by Beauville. However, the Grothendieck–Mumford correspondence is likely already published (Mumford, Selected Papers II), so it is probably not entirely missed.
